lede: Heat blue copper sulfate crystals and they turn white; drip water on and the blue floods back. Some reactions run both ways, and which way they seem to go is decided by the conditions you set.
can: Write a reversible reaction with the equilibrium sign and say what it means.
Describe the copper(II) sulfate demonstration in both directions.
Define dynamic equilibrium the way the mark scheme wants it.

md: Most reactions you have met run one way and stop. Some run both ways: the products turn back into the reactants, and which way the reaction seems to go depends on the conditions you choose. Blue crystals going white in a test tube is the demonstration to keep in your head.

prompt: In the demonstration above, what colour is the solid after the blue crystals have been heated?
explain: White. Heating drives the water out and leaves anhydrous copper(II) sulfate, which is white.

md: A **reversible reaction** is one that can go in **both directions**: the reactants make the products, and the products make the reactants again. It is written with a special arrow, $\ce{<=>}$, instead of the usual one. The **direction** of a reversible reaction can be **changed by altering the reaction conditions** — the temperature, the pressure or the concentration.

title: Why the arrow is worth a mark on its own
md: A one-way arrow says the reaction finishes and the reactants are gone. The double arrow says something different: both reactions are happening, so reactants and products are present together. The symbol is the claim, which is why schemes give it its own mark.

prompt: Which symbol is used in the equation for a reversible reaction?
explain: The double arrow, ⇌. A single arrow claims the reaction goes one way only, and Summer 2024 examiners recorded the missing equilibrium sign as a lost mark.

md:
**Heat** blue **hydrated copper(II) sulfate** and the water bonded into its crystals is driven off, leaving **white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate**. **Add water** to that white powder and it turns **blue** again, and the tube **gets hot**. One reaction, driven either way by what you do to it:
hydrated copper(II) sulfate $\ce{<=>}$ anhydrous copper(II) sulfate + water, or $\ce{CuSO4.5H2O <=> CuSO4 + 5H2O}$.

prompt: Water is added to white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate. State the colour change you would see: white to ______.
explain: White to blue. Say both colours: an answer that gives only one of them earns nothing, and Summer 2024 examiners reported a wide range of wrong colours here.

md: Start a reversible reaction in a **closed system** and two things happen at once. The forward reaction begins fast and slows down as the reactants are used up; the reverse reaction begins at zero and speeds up as products build. Here the forward rate falls from 10 and the reverse rate climbs from 0 until, at 60 s, both are 4. From that moment on the reaction is at **dynamic equilibrium**.

prompt: On the graph above, at what time, in seconds, do the forward and reverse rates first become equal?
explain: 60 s. Before that the forward rate is the larger; afterwards the two curves run along together.

md:
**The question.** Complete the sentence: a dynamic equilibrium occurs in a closed system when … **[2]**
**Step 1 — the rates, not the amounts.** The first half is *the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal*. It is the **rates** that are equal, never the amounts of the two substances.
**Step 2 — what that does to the amounts.** The second half is *the amounts of reactants and products remain constant*.

prompt: Which pair of statements completes the definition of dynamic equilibrium in a closed system?
options: the forward and reverse rates are equal, and the amounts of reactants and products stay constant
the amounts of reactants and products are equal, and the reaction has stopped
the forward reaction has finished, and the reverse reaction takes over
answer: the forward and reverse rates are equal, and the amounts of reactants and products stay constant
explain: Rates equal, amounts constant. Equal amounts is a different claim and is not what happens, and nothing has stopped — that is what *dynamic* means.

md:
**Step 3 — say why 'dynamic'.** Both reactions are still running at equilibrium, at the same rate as each other. Nothing has stopped: it only looks still from outside.
**Step 4 — say why 'closed'.** In an open container a gas escapes and cannot react back, so the reverse reaction never catches up and no equilibrium is reached.

title: What lost the mark here
md: In Summer 2024's C2 Higher paper most wrong answers said the **concentration stayed put** and stopped there, leaving out the **equal rates** that the scheme looks for first. Write the rates first, the amounts second.

prompt: At dynamic equilibrium in a closed system, the ______ of the forward and reverse reactions are equal.
explain: Rates. Equal rates are what keep the amounts constant, and they are what the scheme looks for first.

md: Altering the **temperature**, the **pressure** or the **concentration** changes the direction a reversible reaction goes, and so changes how much product is present. Almost everyone names temperature; the marks are usually in the other two, so learn all three as a set.

title: Not on this specification
md: Other boards ask which **way** the equilibrium shifts when a condition changes, using Le Chatelier's principle, and set the conditions used in the Haber process. CCEA's Double Award specification stops at *the direction can be changed by altering the conditions*: you are never asked to predict which way.

prompt: Besides temperature, which conditions can be altered to change the direction of a reversible reaction?
explain: Pressure and concentration. Summer 2025 records that most candidates named temperature and few named either of the other two.

md:
say what a **reversible reaction** is, and write it with the $\ce{<=>}$ sign.
name the three conditions that change the direction: **temperature, pressure, concentration**.
describe the copper(II) sulfate demonstration both ways, with the **blue** and **white** colours the right way round.
define **dynamic equilibrium**: in a closed system, the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal and the amounts of reactants and products remain constant.
say why the system must be **closed** and why the equilibrium is called **dynamic**.

Equilibrium closes the C2 paper. The first mark is usually the equilibrium sign in an equation; the last is the definition, where **rates** must come before amounts. Stuck? Write what is equal and what is constant, in that order. The Sheet below lists the traps.
